slides.alt: Shop shelves full of different kinds of flour. Text: It all starts at the grocery store, with so many varieties of flour to choose from.
Bags of wholegrain rye and wheat flour on a shelf. Text: I love rye, so naturally I choose Roggen Vollkorn Mehl (wholegrain rye) and stock up my pantry.
An empty labelled jar with rye flour bags, a thermometer and a spoon. Text: In bread making, I am religious about exact measurements and temperatures.
The jar with rye flour on a kitchen scale. Text: I start with 20 g of flour and 20 ml of water.
Short video of water being poured into the jar with rye flour.
Short video of flour and water being stirred together in the jar.
A hand holding the jar with the freshly mixed starter. Text: After mixing it well, I put it in the warmest place in the house, at 22 to 24 degrees.
Two jars resting on a radiator under a checked tea towel. Text: And then I wait... a little giddy. Will it grow?
The two jars by the window, seen a little closer. Text: Hours later, the first signs of fermentation. Yaay!
Close-up of the two jars with the starter rising. Text: And so it goes, for days. Some days look different, and some jars lag behind.
A hand holding the jar with the first bubbles and a yellow rubber band. Text: But I always come back: 20 g starter, 20 g water, 20 g flour, until the culture grows stronger.
The jar with a yellow rubber band marking the level. Text: I mark the level to see my progress.
The jar with a blue rubber band marking the level. Text: I already start using it in breads, though I top it off with dry yeast, just in case.
The risen, bubbly starter in the jar. Text: Growing my own starter is more than a daily ritual. Somehow, it is truly soul-nourishing.
